name: Leola Data Center
heading: 3. Leola Data Center — 50 MW Proposed, Local Permit Pending
brief: A proposed 50 MW data center near Leola in McPherson County would occupy a site west of the town near 116th Street and 358th Avenue. Dakota News Now reported that county planners deferred a conditional-use permit decision in August after residents questioned the facility’s water needs and its implications for nearby farms and livestock. The project is proposed—not an operating installation. Its electric-service arrangements made progress, but that did not settle its local approval. The South Dakota Public Utilities Commission’s docket EL24-027 records a September 11 order assigning Montana-Dakota Utilities as the project’s electric provider under a settlement with FEM Electric. County officials still must evaluate land-use permission; electric service assignment does not itself authorize construction. The Dakota Scout reported that officials wanted enforceable agreements governing proposed financial contributions before voting. name: Big Watt Digital, Sully County
heading: 2. Big Watt Digital, Sully County — 300 MW Expansion Target; About 30 MW Operating
brief: Near Onida, approximately 23 miles north of Pierre, Big Watt Digital operates a roughly 30 MW Bitcoin mining facility . It is the state’s largest operating data center identified by the Legislative Research Council , even though its active size is far below the much larger proposals appearing elsewhere. Bitcoin mining equipment performs repeated SHA-256 hashing rather than general-purpose AI training, but both activities need substantial electrical infrastructure and cooling. The project’s 300 MW future expansion was reported by South Dakota Searchlight on January 30 , which interviewed utility and county officials. That projection is included in the planned-capacity ranking, with an important limitation: public reporting did not establish that the full 300 MW expansion had been built, energized, or assigned a binding delivery schedule by October. Big Watt therefore should not be described as a 300 MW operating mine. The facility illustrates the tangible effects of an operating project. name: xAI Colossus 1, Memphis
heading: 3. xAI Colossus 1, Memphis — 280 MW Reported; Operating
brief: The original Colossus complex occupies the former Electrolux appliance manufacturing plant on Paul R. Lowry Road in southwest Memphis. It became operational in 2024, after the company rapidly installed an enormous cluster of Nvidia GPUs. The Tennessee fiscal note reported 280 MW of capacity for the original Memphis data center, but that does not mean the utility was supplying 280 MW continuously. The distinction matters because the Tennessee Valley Authority approved an initial 150 MW firm power commitment through Memphis Light, Gas and Water, while xAI also used battery systems and gas turbines. The underlying utility and permitting record distinguishes authorized grid power, turbine generation and facility demand. Their different capacities should not be added as if every megawatt were running servers full time. name: Meta Gallatin
heading: 2. Meta Gallatin — 300 MW Reported; Operating
brief: Meta’s Gallatin Data Center began serving internet traffic on November 14, 2024 , after breaking ground in 2020. The 300 MW site capacity cited in Tennessee’s fiscal review places it slightly above the original Colossus facility on that published baseline. The figure is not a disclosure that 300 MW of GPUs or servers are currently in use. Meta says the Gallatin project represents more than $1.5 billion in investment at full buildout and supports more than 100 operational jobs. Its data halls serve the infrastructure behind Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and other Meta services. In a contrasting technical estimate, Epoch AI’s October 5 model suggests roughly 87 MW of active IT power ; that is an independent estimate, not Meta’s reported electrical site rating. name: xAI Colossus 2, Memphis
heading: 1. xAI Colossus 2, Memphis — 1,563 MW Planned in State Report; Partially Operational
brief: The second Colossus development, near Tulane Road and Whitehaven in Memphis, dwarfs the other two sites on Tennessee’s reported planning figures. The state’s February fiscal note assigned it 1,563 MW of planned capacity and anticipated a 2026 start. Subsequent reporting and independent assessments indicate that parts of the campus are now operating, with more infrastructure still being built. The 1,563 MW figure is a planned site rating , not a confirmed current grid draw. Epoch AI’s July 30 assessment estimated about 946 MW of installed IT power at Colossus 2 and projected further growth into 2027, using satellite imagery, cooling-system modeling and company disclosures. That is a different method from a facility’s planned electrical capacity; neither number should be presented as a measured utility demand. The project’s actual deployed GPU inventory and energization will continue to change as construction progresses. name: Stargate Abilene
heading: 7. Stargate Abilene — 1.2 GW Planned Campus; Partly Operating
brief: The flagship Stargate development at Abilene is one of the state’s clearest examples of the difference between a planned megaproject and equipment already running. Satellite analysis from Epoch AI, updated October 28 , estimates 618 MW of current IT power supporting AI hardware, with more expected as construction proceeds. This is an independent model, not a company meter reading. Unlike a raw development announcement, the facility’s already-running sections demonstrate that an extensive portion of its infrastructure has reached commercial service.
